item.content:encoded:
The United States Department of the Interior held the first offshore critical minerals lease sale in the country’s history on November 19, 2026, auctioning about 31.5 million acres of seabed off American Samoa for $6 million in high bids. The sale came three days after a federal judge in Honolulu threw out the endangered species approval behind it.

On November 16, Judge Jill Otake of the US District Court for the District of Hawaii ruled that the United States National Marine Fisheries Service violated the Endangered Species Act by considering only the preliminary surveys the leases would allow and not the exploration and mining that could follow. She vacated the agency’s Letter of Concurrence, its finding that the sale was not likely to adversely affect protected species, but the order did not include an injunction against the auction.

Earthjustice, the environmental law organization that brought the case, said in a statement sent to Pasquines that the Department of the Interior’s Marine Minerals Administration “ignored the court’s ruling and proceeded with an illegal lease sale.” “In deciding to move forward with today’s scheduled sale, the Trump administration has performed a renegade, unlawful act,” Earthjustice attorney Chris Eaton said. “We will use the full extent of the law to vigorously push for the leases to be voided.”

What was sold

The two lease areas lie 150 to 240 miles east of Pago Pago, in waters 4,630 to 20,100 feet deep, according to the Department of the Interior. The leases carry a 20-year primary term and royalties of 2% for the first five years of production and 5% after that. The minimum bid was $3 million per area, according to the final leasing notice published in October.

The department did not name the winning bidders or mention the court ruling. It said results would be posted online, with a final statistical summary within 90 days, and that the leases do not authorize delineation, testing, or mining, which would require further environmental reviews and approvals. “This is the first time the United States has held an offshore critical minerals lease sale in the Pacific,” Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum said. Mike Olsen, acting director of the Marine Minerals Administration, said any future development would be subject to rigorous safety and environmental standards.

Wetstone US Ventures, a deep-sea mining startup, won both areas at the $3 million minimum, the Associated Press reported. Two bidders attended the auction, held at the Ventura County Fire Department headquarters in Southern California, but only Wetstone placed bids, while a few dozen protesters gathered outside.

The sale traces to an unsolicited request from Impossible Metals Inc., an American mining company, and to Executive Order 14285 on offshore critical minerals, which President Donald Trump (R) signed in April 2025.

Bidders “on notice”

Before the auction, a Marine Minerals Administration spokesperson told The Hill that the agency “is aware of the opinion.” “We are currently working to address the issues raised in the court’s opinion,” the spokesperson said.

Otake had anticipated the possibility. In a related case, she wrote that if she vacated the review and the administration went ahead with the sale, “any bidders for the leases will be on notice that the Court has determined that NMFS violated the Endangered Species Act,” The Hill reported. Earthjustice attorney David Henkin issued a similar warning, telling The Hill that “if you buy those leases knowing that they haven’t complied with the Endangered Species Act, do not be surprised if the court later sets aside voids, vacates, throws into the garbage can those leases.”

In a statement, the Marine Minerals Administration said it had addressed the court’s opinion by starting to consult with the fisheries service on another environmental assessment, the AP reported. It did not cancel or delay the auction.

A second lawsuit, filed October 19 by Faleula o le Manu‘atele, a council of chiefs from the Manu‘a Islands, along with Fa‘asao Amerika Samoa and the Conservation Council for Hawai‘i, argues that the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act does not authorize mineral leasing in US territories, including American Samoa.

A territory divided

American Samoa’s leaders have taken different positions. A day before the sale, Governor Pulaali’i Nikolao Pula (R) called it “a historic moment for American Samoa and for our nation.” “Let me be clear: this is not approval to mine our ocean floor,” he said. “American Samoa must not simply be a spectator in decisions affecting our ocean and our future.” His administration is exploring positioning Pago Pago as a regional maritime and logistics hub for deep-sea minerals activity, and he called for federal help to rehabilitate the port.

Delegate Aumua Amata Coleman Radewagen (R) has said her opposition to seabed mining has not changed. “I represent our people, and most of our people are opposed,” she said in July. The Marine Minerals Administration received more than 76,000 public comments on the sale, the overwhelming majority opposed, according to the Natural Resources Defense Council, an environmental advocacy group. “Deep-sea mining is not the future we want for American Samoa,” said Sabrina Suluai-Mahuka, founder of Finafinau, a youth-centered environmental organization in American Samoa. “We had hoped it would never come to this,” Suluai-Mahuka said after the sale, the AP reported.

Ocean Conservancy, an environmental advocacy group, said the seabed went for 20 cents per acre. “From Alaska to American Samoa, the people most affected by these lease sales have long and firmly maintained: ‘not in our waters,’” said ‘Wáahlaal Gíidaak, the group’s vice president of Arctic and Northern Waters.

The Marianas sale is next

The administration plans a second sale on December 16 for seabed off the Northern Mariana Islands and Guam, where the closest lease area lies about 47 miles from Guam. The same lawyers have asked Otake to throw out the National Marine Fisheries Service’s approval for that sale on the same grounds, and Earthjustice attorney Harley Broyles told The Guam Daily Post in October that she anticipated “a similar or like ruling.”

Any leases that are issued could also become harder to undo. Earthjustice has argued that a provision in the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a permitting bill the US Senate advanced on November 16, could lock in such leases by barring future administrations from revoking or altering them except in limited circumstances.

item.content:encoded:
The United States Senate voted 70 to 27 on November 16, 2026, to end debate on a revised version of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), clearing the way for a final vote as early as this week. The bill would rewrite how federal agencies review and approve projects across the country, and environmental lawyers representing groups in American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands warn that one provision could make it far harder for a future administration to undo the seabed mining leases the federal government is preparing to sell off both territories.

S 5653 was introduced on September 30 by Senator Shelley Moore Capito (R) of West Virginia, Senator Mike Lee (R) of Utah, Senator Sheldon Whitehouse (D) of Rhode Island, and Senator Martin Heinrich (D) of New Mexico. Its nearly 500 pages would change the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the National Historic Preservation Act, the Honolulu Star-Advertiser reported, and would also speed approvals for power lines and pipelines and require data centers to pay for the grid upgrades they need, according to Inside Climate News. “I urge the swift passage of BAAJA to make life more affordable for American families,” Capito said when the sponsors released a revised version on November 7.

The territories have no senators to vote on it. If the bill reaches the US House of Representatives, their five members there can vote in committee but not on final passage.

Leases that would be hard to take back

The provision at the center of those warnings is Section 1401, labeled “project certainty.” As introduced, it would bar federal agencies from revoking, suspending, or altering a federal permit or authorization except in limited cases, such as a court order, a permit violation, fraud, a request from the permit holder, or certain threats to life, property, national security, or defense, according to the Congressional Research Service. Plaintiffs who win a lawsuit to enforce the section could recover 25% to 50% of total project costs from the Judgment Fund, a permanent federal appropriation.

Earthjustice, the environmental law organization representing plaintiffs in lawsuits over planned lease sales off American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands, argues that the provision would cover those leases. Section 1401 “will effectively lock in this administration’s decisions, whether good or bad,” Earthjustice legislative director Addie Haughey wrote on November 5. Once leases exist, she wrote, the bill “could block a future administration from reversing the leases or even adding environmentally protective conditions to them, regardless of the science or new policies to protect affected communities.”

On November 16, a federal judge in Honolulu ruled that the United States National Marine Fisheries Service violated the Endangered Species Act when it approved the first such sale, scheduled for November 19 off American Samoa. A second sale off the Northern Mariana Islands is set for December 16, with its closest lease area about 47 miles from Guam. Federal officials say a lease authorizes only preliminary work, such as mapping and sampling, and that any mining would need a separate plan and environmental review. Governor Lou Leon Guerrero (D) of Guam asked the US Department of the Interior’s Marine Minerals Administration in an October 20 letter to pause the Marianas sale until Guam has a meaningful say.

The November 7 revision changed parts of Section 1401. It added “human health, the environment” to the harms that would allow an agency to alter a permit, but only to prevent “immediate, specific, urgent, substantial, and proximate harm or damage,” and clarified that agencies could act in response to court decisions, Earthjustice wrote in its analysis of the changes. The group said the revision still leaves the “forever permits” issue unfixed.

Species reviews in the territories

The bill’s Endangered Species Act changes would also reach the territories, which the act already counts as states. The current definition lists Puerto Rico, American Samoa, the US Virgin Islands, Guam, and the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands. BAAJA would replace that last entry with the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, a change the Congressional Research Service said would “reflect changes in the status” of the Northern Mariana Islands.

The bill would shorten the deadline for formal consultations, in which wildlife agencies review projects that could harm protected species, from 90 days to 60 days. It would create a program allowing states to take over consultations now conducted by the United States Fish and Wildlife Service if they can show the financial, personnel, and legal resources to do so. It would also require anyone challenging a biological opinion to file in the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit within 150 days. Under current law, such opinions can be challenged in federal district courts within six years. Earthjustice said the November 7 revision made “no substantial improvements” to the bill’s Endangered Species Act provisions.

Tribal nations and Native Hawaiians

Much of the criticism has come from environmental and tribal groups. As introduced, the bill would rewrite Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act, which requires federal agencies to weigh effects on historic properties, by narrowing the projects subject to review, defining which effects count as “adverse,” setting deadlines, limiting judicial review, and limiting when agencies must consult state and tribal historic preservation officers, according to the Congressional Research Service.

Eleven tribal organizations, including the National Congress of American Indians, the Native American Rights Fund, and the All Pueblo Council of Governors, asked Congress on November 8 to hold the bill until the next Congress or remove its historic preservation title. “Tribal sovereignty, meaningful consultation, and the protection of sacred places are not negotiable,” they wrote. National Congress of American Indians President Mark Macarro said, “This bill is rotten from the inside and there is no fixing the rot.”

The November 7 revision dropped a section saying agencies “may consult” with tribal nations and a provision that would have narrowed which sites qualify as properties of traditional religious or cultural importance, Earthjustice wrote, but the group said the core problems remain. “I’ve worked hard to incorporate the feedback we’ve heard from Tribes and New Mexicans into this Substitute Amendment,” Heinrich said. The bill would also let tribes grant rights-of-way across their lands without approval from the Secretary of the Interior if their own regulations are approved, and would authorize $200 million a year for the Historic Preservation Fund and $20 million a year for a competitive grant program for tribal historic preservation officers.

The same historic preservation law requires agencies to consult Native Hawaiian organizations, and advocates in Hawaii have raised similar concerns. Senator Mazie Hirono (D) of Hawaii voted against advancing the bill on November 9, while Senator Brian Schatz (D) of Hawaii voted for it, the Star-Advertiser reported. “We need impacted communities to be consulted earlier,” said Davis Price, a senior domestic policy strategist at NDN Collective. Senator Ben Ray Luján (D) of New Mexico was among 27 Democrats who voted against ending debate on November 16.

A race against the calendar

The sponsors want the bill passed before Democrats take control of both chambers on January 3, 2027. If the US Senate approves it, it would go to the Republican-led US House. US House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D) of New York wants changes, Inside Climate News reported, and Representative Jared Huffman (D) of California, the top Democrat on the US House Committee on Natural Resources, has urged the US Senate to wait and revisit the bill in the next Congress, when Democrats will have more leverage. The American Federation of Labor and Congress of Industrial Organizations has endorsed the bill as a “critical first step towards meeting the moment on affordability, jobs, and environment,” while former Vice President Al Gore (D) called passing it a “serious mistake.”

item.content:encoded:
Governor-elect Stacey Plaskett (D) of the US Virgin Islands has stood by her choice of Dean Plaskett, a former commissioner convicted in 2008 of bribery and obstruction of justice, as chief of staff of the team preparing her administration to take office on January 4, 2027. “He has served his sentence, and that chapter of his life does not erase the experience, knowledge, and abilities he brings to his work,” she said in a statement.

The appointment has shadowed the start of the transition for Plaskett, who won 62.8% of the vote on November 3 with running mate US Virgin Islands Senate President Milton Potter (D) after a campaign that promised to restore public confidence, strengthen accountability, and address corruption. The Virgin Islands Daily News described him as her cousin, while the transition team declined to answer the St. Thomas Source’s questions about any family relationship.

A contracting scheme and a nine-year sentence

Dean Plaskett led the US Virgin Islands Department of Planning and Natural Resources from 1999 to 2007. On February 27, 2008, a federal jury convicted him of one count of bribery concerning programs receiving federal funds and two counts of obstruction of justice, acquitting him of the other charges in a 12-count indictment, the VI Consortium reported. The case involved more than $1.4 million in public contracts, with payments of more than $1 million going to work that was largely or entirely never done. The bribery count centered on a $650,000 contract awarded to a shell company.

After the territory’s inspector general opened an investigation into at least one of the contracts, he “spearheaded an illicit scheme designed to thwart any investigation into the matter” by creating and backdating documents, engaging in a “sham internal agency investigation,” lying to law enforcement officials, and giving false testimony to a grand jury, the Source reported. He was sentenced in August 2008 to 108 months in federal prison, three years of supervised release, and a personal judgment of $1,086,237.34. His co-defendant, former US Virgin Islands Commissioner of Property and Procurement Marc Biggs, was also convicted, and a federal appeals court upheld both men’s convictions. The US Virgin Islands Supreme Court ordered Dean Plaskett disbarred on March 13, 2012.

After returning to the territory, he obtained a license for a consulting company and was hired as territorial director of Facilities Management at the US Virgin Islands Port Authority under former Executive Director Carlton Dowe, the Daily News reported. Dowe was indicted in March in a federal case involving loan application fraud.

“This is not a position he wanted”

In an interview with the St. Thomas Source, the governor-elect said she had asked him to serve. “This is not a position he wanted,” she said. “It’s something that I asked him to do, because I know he’s going to give me unvarnished truth.” She pointed to his leadership of her campaign and argued that previous administrations had appointed people with criminal histories and that her decisions face different scrutiny. Transition positions are unpaid, the Source noted. His role after the transition has not been decided. “For now, he’s the chief of staff of the transition, and we’ll see where that goes,” she said.

Plaskett described the job as temporary, serving as a liaison between her and transition staff while she continues serving as delegate to Congress. Transition director Erwin Raphael, a former automotive executive raised on St. Croix, said he runs the operation. “The transition process, the transition teams and what we’re doing during the transition reports to me,” Raphael said. When pressed, Plaskett did not commit to keeping people with past corruption convictions out of her permanent administration.

The appointment also drew a Change.org petition. The petition, started on November 7 by Catharine Chandler, titled “Ensure transparency and reject nepotism in USVI government,” asked Plaskett and Potter to revoke the appointment and had 212 verified signatures by the next evening. It called the choice “a slap in the face to every Virgin Island voter who demanded change and fiscal responsibility.”

On November 12, the VI Consortium reported that Dean Plaskett, who had taken leave from the Port Authority and planned to resign before the new administration, would instead return to the agency, citing people with knowledge of the matter. The outlet said it was unclear whether he had given up the transition post. As of November 18, the transition’s website still listed him as transition chief of staff.

An ethics bill on day one

Plaskett has acknowledged the distrust behind the reaction. US Virgin Islanders “have been and continue to be traumatized by the indictments, convictions, corruption that is perceived in our government and may be actual,” she said. She pledged to send ethics legislation to the Legislature of the US Virgin Islands on inauguration day, including mandatory training, financial disclosures for senior unclassified officials, an independent white-collar crime division within the US Virgin Islands Department of Justice, and a say for the Legislature in hiring or firing the attorney general.

Asked about former officials convicted of felonies returning to government work, she said she would call the 37th Legislature into a Committee of the Whole to hold hearings and bring forward laws that clearly state “what positions people can and cannot have, what ethics rules we should follow, what people can accept and not accept.” A legal team is reviewing the ethical standards of transition members, she said. “We were very careful in ensuring that no one on that team has any pecuniary interest,” Plaskett said.

Plaskett’s own judgment has faced scrutiny before. In 2019, during a US House hearing, she exchanged text messages with Jeffrey Epstein, a convicted sex offender who owned two islands in the territory, and a resolution to censure her over it failed in the US House on November 18, 2025. She has denied any wrongdoing.

Plans to reshape government

The transition, which announced its leadership on November 5, has 14 policy committees reviewing government operations and preparing recommendations for the first 100 days, with landing teams to gather information inside agencies. Plaskett has described the traditional transition as “plug and play” and said she wants to examine whether the government’s structure fits the services residents need before filling positions.

Potter is leading a restructuring review that is looking at combining roles to pay people more, using artificial intelligence for some tasks, and moving some functions between agencies or outside government, according to the Source. Plaskett has also proposed a 311 line for nonemergency government services, a teachers corps to recruit recent graduates, and conditions on a proposed $250 million bond package, including tying aid to the territory’s hospitals to billing improvements and barring spending before the new administration takes office.

Plaskett will remain the territory’s delegate in the US House of Representatives until former Senator Janelle Sarauw (D), who won the seat on November 3, takes office. She and Potter succeed Governor Albert Bryan Jr. (D) on January 4, 2027.

item.content:encoded:
A federal judge in Honolulu ruled on November 16, 2026, that the United States National Marine Fisheries Service violated the Endangered Species Act when it signed off on the first deep-sea mining lease sale in the United States, an auction of seabed off American Samoa scheduled for November 19. Judge Jill Otake of the US District Court for the District of Hawaii found that the agency looked only at the preliminary surveys the leases would allow and “did not even attempt to consider the potential effects of post-leasing activities,” including exploration and mining.

Otake granted summary judgment to Fa‘asao Amerika Samoa and the Conservation Council for Hawai‘i, which sued on August 18 with lawyers from the environmental law organization Earthjustice, and vacated the agency’s Letter of Concurrence, the February 2026 finding that the sale was not likely to adversely affect protected species. She called the agency’s “cramped, expedited, informal consultation” apparently unprecedented for leasing on the outer continental shelf and described its error as “fundamental.” The government had asked her to leave the letter in place while the agency fixed it, but she wrote that the National Marine Fisheries Service “needs to do the bulk of its consultation duty for the first time.”

The order vacated the letter and did not include an injunction against the auction. Bloomberg Law reported that the administration may not legally proceed with auctioning the more than 31 million acres. As of November 17, the Marine Minerals Administration’s website still listed the sale for November 19.

What the leases would allow

The Marine Minerals Administration, the United States Department of the Interior agency that replaced the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management this year, plans to offer two lease areas of about 16.3 million and 15.2 million acres, with a minimum bid of $3 million each, for polymetallic nodules and ferromanganese crusts on the seafloor. The federal government opened the process in June 2025 in response to an unsolicited request from Impossible Metals Inc., an American mining company, according to the ruling, less than two months after President Donald Trump (R) signed Executive Order 14285 on offshore critical minerals.

A lease would at first allow only surveys, mapping, and limited sampling. Exploration, testing, and commercial mining would each require a separate plan, environmental review, and approval. Federal attorneys called the risk to protected species at the lease stage “virtually nonexistent,” while Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum told G20 energy ministers on September 14 that seabed mining permits could be issued “within months.”

Otake found that the National Marine Fisheries Service had to weigh the effects of the entire action, which she described as deep-sea mining of the outer continental shelf near American Samoa. The area under review is home to several dozen species listed under the Endangered Species Act, including blue, fin, sei, and sperm whales; green, hawksbill, loggerhead, leatherback, and olive ridley sea turtles; oceanic whitetip and scalloped hammerhead sharks; giant manta rays; the chambered nautilus; and five species of coral, according to the ruling.

“This ruling is a win for communities in American Samoa, as well as the whales, sharks, and sea turtles who call the waters surrounding these islands home,” Earthjustice attorney Chris Eaton said. “American Samoans share a profound cultural and spiritual bond with the ocean, which Samoans have stewarded for thousands of years. We are relieved by this ruling,” said Seumalu Dr. Elora Raymond, a cofounder of Fa‘asao Amerika Samoa.

A territory with limited say

American Samoa’s elected leaders can comment on the sale, but the decision rests with federal officials. Delegate Aumua Amata Coleman Radewagen (R), who cannot vote on the final passage of bills in the US House of Representatives, said in July that her opposition to seabed mining had not changed. “I represent our people, and most of our people are opposed,” she said.

Governor Pulaali’i Nikolao Pula (R), who secured a longer comment period in 2025, focused his September 15 comments to federal regulators on conditions. He wrote that the lease “does not itself authorize commercial mining” and that “American Samoa supports maintaining this distinction,” and asked that any preliminary work be used for research and monitoring. “Tuna supports thousands of livelihoods directly and indirectly and remains central to American Samoa’s economic security,” he wrote. The Marine Minerals Administration recommended accepting his comments “with qualification,” according to an agency decision memo that quotes his letter.

In a statement dated November 16, the same day as the ruling, Pula welcomed the sale as “a historic moment for American Samoa and for our nation.” “Let me be clear: this is not approval to mine our ocean floor,” he said, calling it an opportunity “to learn what resources may exist, understand the environment in which they are found, and determine whether future development can occur responsibly.” He pointed to population decline, limited economic diversification, and the reduction of temporary federal funding. “We cannot afford to stand still while our economy continues to face serious challenges,” he said. The statement, which did not mention the ruling, also said his administration is exploring ways to position Pago Pago as a regional maritime and logistics hub for deep-sea minerals activities.

A second lawsuit, filed October 19, raises a broader question. Faleula o le Manu‘atele, a council of matai, or chiefs, from the Manu‘a Islands, joined the two groups in arguing that the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act does not authorize mineral leasing in US territories and that treaty requirements must be met before leasing can occur in American Samoa.

The Marianas are next

The ruling also bears on the Northern Mariana Islands and Guam, where the Marine Minerals Administration plans a second sale on December 16. In a footnote, Otake noted that the same lawyers represent plaintiffs in a similar case over that sale, filed on behalf of Our Common Wealth 670, PåganWatch, the Conservation Council for Hawai‘i, and the Center for Biological Diversity. They ask her to vacate an August 10 letter in which the National Marine Fisheries Service reached the same conclusion for the Marianas. “I imagine that we can anticipate a similar or like ruling in CNMI,” Earthjustice attorney Harley Broyles told The Guam Daily Post in October, though she added that she could not speak for the court. Earthjustice attorney David Henkin discussed what the American Samoa ruling means for the Marianas in an interview with Marianas Press.

Both governors in the Marianas have asked federal regulators to hold off on that sale. Governor Lou Leon Guerrero (D) of Guam asked the Marine Minerals Administration in an October 20 letter to pause it. Governor David M. Apatang (I) of the Northern Mariana Islands, who had declined to ask the US Department of the Interior for a pause, saying he wanted to see how the lawsuits were decided, encouraged federal officials in October 16 comments to pause the leasing process until the two cases in Hawaii are resolved, while also seeking revenue sharing and safeguards. Leon Guerrero has said Guam was not consulted before the federal government sought information on deep-sea mining in the region. “We are not a sovereign nation, so we have no control,” she said.

Delegate Kimberlyn King-Hinds (R) of the Northern Mariana Islands has introduced the Pacific Minerals Economic Security Act, which would send 50% of revenue from covered leases to eligible adjacent territorial governments, strengthen financial assurance and environmental bonding requirements, and expand notification and consultation requirements. “While I do not support or oppose seabed mining, we must recognize the nation’s strategic imperative to develop secure critical mineral supply chains,” she said, adding that the bill “would provide a crucial insurance policy for the Pacific territories that could be directly affected.”

item.content:encoded:
The Democratic Party of the Northern Mariana Islands endorsed Northern Mariana Islands Representative Blas Jonathan “BJ” Attao (I) and CNMI House Speaker Edmund Villagomez (I) on November 12, 2026, in their runoff for governor against former Governor Ralph DLG Torres (R) and his running mate, Benjamin Jones Jr. (R). A week earlier, the Northern Mariana Islands Office of the Attorney General took its fight over the settlement of Torres’s criminal case to the CNMI Supreme Court, appealing a ruling that upheld the deal.

The runoff is set for November 20. Torres and Jones led the November 3 general election with 6,437 votes, or 49.5%, 72 votes short of the majority needed to avoid a second round, while Attao and Villagomez received 5,043 votes, or 38.7%. Voters will also decide the commonwealth’s first runoff for attorney general, in which the former governor’s brother, Joaquin DLG Torres, finished first.

Democrats point to the Torres years

“The people of the CNMI have already lived through the Torres administration, and we cannot afford to go back,” party chair Annie Pickelsimer said in a statement announcing the endorsement at the Attao-Villagomez campaign headquarters. She pointed to “nearly half a million dollars in public money spent on the former governor’s travel, including first-class tickets for himself and his wife,” and said Torres had refused to appear before the committee of the Northern Mariana Islands House of Representatives that investigated that spending.

Attao chaired that committee and voted to impeach Torres, according to the party. “Public funds are a public trust, and our families deserve leaders who treat them that way,” Pickelsimer said. The Attao-Villagomez ticket has also been endorsed by Governor David M. Apatang (I), who took office in July 2025 after the death of Governor Arnold I. Palacios (I) and was not on this year’s ballot, and by former Delegate Gregorio Kilili Camacho Sablan (D), who represented the islands in Congress for 16 years.

Democrats had also endorsed Galvin Sablan Deleon Guerrero, the president of Northern Marianas College, for delegate. He lost on November 3 to Delegate Kimberlyn King-Hinds (R), who won a second term in the United States House of Representatives with 63.7% of the vote.

The mayors line up behind Torres

Torres has the support of the mayors of all four of the commonwealth’s municipalities. Saipan Mayor Ramon “RB” Camacho (I), Tinian and Aguiguan Mayor Edwin Aldan (R), Rota Mayor Aubry Hocog (R), and Northern Islands Mayor Valentino Taisacan Jr. (I) endorsed Torres and Jones in a joint statement on November 16. “At this critical moment for our Commonwealth, we believe Ralph Torres and Benjamin M. Jones, Jr. offer the leadership, experience, and stability needed to move the Northern Mariana Islands forward,” they said.

The mayors said it was important to elect leaders who will work with municipal governments and make sure the needs of Saipan, Tinian, Rota, and the Northern Islands are reflected in policy and development decisions. They listed strengthening the economy, improving infrastructure, supporting education and health care, and managing government resources responsibly among their priorities. Torres was governor from December 2015 to January 2023, and Jones is the principal of Kagman High School.

Whoever wins will govern islands whose visitor arrivals fell 32% in fiscal year 2025, according to the Marianas Visitors Authority, and where Super Typhoon Sinlaku destroyed the homes of thousands of residents on Saipan and Tinian in April, prompting a major disaster declaration.

The third ticket stays out

The candidates who finished third will not pick a side. Former Education Commissioner Lawrence F. Camacho (I) and former Northern Mariana Islands Senate President Edith Deleon Guerrero (I), who received 1,537 votes, or 11.8%, said on November 8 that they would not endorse either ticket. “The votes that were entrusted to our campaign belong to you. They are not ours to give away, trade, or direct toward another candidate,” they said in a signed statement, urging voters to decide “not out of pressure, political loyalty, or personal obligation.”

Early on November 4, Torres said his campaign would reach out to their supporters. “I also embrace what their goals are and how they want to build an economy,” he said.

The appeal

Assistant Attorney General Olga Kelley filed a notice of appeal on November 5, challenging the October 16 decision in which Northern Mariana Islands Superior Court Judge Pro Tempore Arthur R. Barcinas upheld the settlement and the two dismissals with prejudice that followed it, according to court records cited by Marianas Variety.

Torres had faced 12 counts of misconduct in public office, one count of theft related to premium-class travel expenses, and one count of contempt for failing to comply with a legislative subpoena. Under the March 23, 2026, settlement, he agreed to pay $23,745, the difference between premium-class and economy-class airfare, the charges were dismissed with prejudice, and the agreement stated that it should not be construed as an admission of liability or wrongdoing.

Kelley argues that former Assistant Attorney General David Karch, who signed the deal, lacked the authority to grant Torres broad immunity from future civil and criminal liability arising from his time in office. She called Karch’s actions “ultra vires” and contrary to public policy and the public interest, and contends that the agreement effectively shielded the former governor from prosecution for alleged misuse of public funds and other potential wrongdoing tied to his government service through January 9, 2023.

Kelley first moved to undo the agreement on May 29. Barcinas denied the motion in a ten-page decision, ruling that Karch had appeared throughout the case as the commonwealth’s attorney of record, that he had apparent authority to sign the agreement because the commonwealth itself had made him lead prosecutor, and that neither the court nor Torres was ever told his authority had been limited. The judge also found that the dismissals were final judicial orders and that the commonwealth had accepted the benefits of the settlement after Torres met his obligations. Unless the CNMI Supreme Court reverses that ruling, the settlement and dismissals remain in effect.

“I am disappointed that the OAG continues to challenge a settlement negotiated by its own prosecutor, approved by the court, and whose terms I have fully honored,” Torres said in a statement. “In a judicial system governed by the rule of law, the government cannot simply walk away from an agreement because it no longer likes the outcome.”

Premium-class air travel also figured in Torres’s impeachment. The Northern Mariana Islands House of Representatives impeached him on six articles that included allegations of corruption tied to that travel, and in May 2022 the Northern Mariana Islands Senate voted 4 to 3 to acquit him, short of the six votes needed to convict. That November, he lost a runoff to his own lieutenant governor, Palacios, 54.05% to 45.95%.

A first runoff for attorney general

The same ballot will settle the commonwealth’s first runoff for attorney general, an office governors filled by appointment until a 2014 constitutional amendment made it elective. Attorney General Edward Manibusan, who won the first election that year, did not seek reelection, leaving the nonpartisan seat open. Joaquin DLG Torres, the former governor’s brother, led the first round with 5,073 votes, or 39.7%, followed by Michael Evangelista with 3,854 votes, or 30.2%. Jonathan Robert Glass Jr., an assistant attorney general, was eliminated with 3,836 votes, or 30.1%, 18 behind Evangelista. Fewer voters marked a choice in the race: 12,763 voted for attorney general, compared with 13,017 for governor.

Torres, who has practiced law in the commonwealth for decades, told an NMI Bar Association forum on September 12 that the current office had been largely invisible to the public and had engaged in “selective prosecution.” He has clashed with the office over conflict-of-interest questions and said it “doesn’t understand” the issue. In his closing statement, Torres said his representation of the commonwealth would not change regardless of who holds the governor’s office. He made a similar pledge after the general election. “I promise to work with whoever the governor is and make sure that the office has the integrity that is required and be transparent,” he said.

Evangelista, who has worked as both a prosecutor and a private attorney, lost the first attorney general election to Manibusan in 2014. He has described his campaign as protecting the office’s integrity and independence. “I will not promise to prosecute people because of politics, and I will not promise to protect people because of politics. I will follow the evidence, I will follow the law, and I will treat people fairly,” he said at the forum. Glass, who has since endorsed Evangelista in an advertisement run by Evangelista’s campaign, said the office “must remain independent, committed to the rule of law, and focused on serving the people of the commonwealth and not political interests.”

The winner will lead the office that is appealing the ruling in Ralph Torres’s case.

How to vote

Early voting began November 13 and runs through November 19, from 8:30 am to 4 pm, including weekends and the lunch hour, according to the Commonwealth Election Commission. Every registered voter may cast a ballot in the runoff, including those who did not vote on November 3, and voters who requested an absentee ballot for the general election automatically receive one for the runoff. The commission will accept runoff absentee ballots through December 4. On the first day of early voting, 1,094 voters cast ballots—933 on Saipan, 115 on Tinian, and 46 on Rota—and the commission had mailed 1,315 absentee ballots, Executive Director Kayla Igitol Magofna said. Voters must show a photo ID to receive a ballot.

Polls will open from 7 am to 7 pm ChST on November 20, 2026, with results expected soon after.

item.title: 3,755 households on St. Thomas and St. John get automatic SNAP replacement after October outages
item.dc:creator: William-Jose Velez Gonzalez

item.description:
The United States Virgin Islands loaded $539,891 in replacement SNAP benefits onto the cards of 3,755 households on St. Thomas and St. John after the October power outages, with no application required.

The post 3,755 households on St. Thomas and St. John get automatic SNAP replacement after October outages appeared first on Pasquines.
item.content:encoded:
The government of the United States Virgin Islands loaded $539,891 in replacement food benefits onto the cards of 3,755 households on St. Thomas and St. John on November 7, 2026, to cover groceries lost during the power outages that began October 21, the US Virgin Islands Department of Human Services announced. Families did not have to apply. The United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) approved a waiver on November 5 that let the department skip the usual paperwork and pay active Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) households in seven St. Thomas and St. John ZIP codes at once.

Each household received 30% of the SNAP benefits it got in the month before the outages, rounded up to the nearest dollar, or about $144 on average. Governor Albert Bryan Jr. (D) described the relief at his weekly US Virgin Islands Government House briefing on November 9. “For families already struggling to make ends meet, losing a refrigerator full of groceries is a serious financial burden,” he said. “We didn’t want people standing in lines or filling out paperwork to replace food they lost because of the outages.”

Days without power

The outages started the night of October 21. The next day, the US Virgin Islands Water and Power Authority (WAPA) announced rotating outages across St. Thomas and St. John, blaming problems with two generating units. Districtwide outages followed on October 23 and 24, and WAPA did not restore all its feeders until late on October 24, Pasquines reported. Bryan authorized Human Services Commissioner Averil George to seek federal approval to help SNAP recipients who lost food.

Under federal rules, a household that loses food bought with SNAP benefits must report the loss within ten days and return a signed statement within ten days of that report, and the replacement cannot exceed one month’s benefits. The waiver removed those steps for the district. “By securing this federal waiver, we were able to completely automate the replacement process, bypassing the standard requirement for individual households to visit our offices and sign affidavits,” George said.

The US Virgin Islands and Guam take part in SNAP, while Puerto Rico receives a federal block grant for its own Nutrition Assistance Program. More than 15,000 Virgin Islanders rely on SNAP, out of a population of about 87,000, the VI Consortium reported in July 2025. The territory will soon pay more to run the program. Under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed that month, the federal share of SNAP administrative costs falls from 50% to 25% starting in 2027, and beginning in fiscal year 2028, states and territories with payment error rates above 6% will have to cover part of the benefits.

Bryan thanked George’s team and acknowledged that the territory still needs more reliable electricity. Repairs to key generating units and new temporary generation for St. Thomas and St. John are not expected before 2027.

Opportunity Zones in all three islands

At the same briefing, Bryan said the US Department of the Treasury had approved all 18 census tracts his administration nominated as Opportunity Zones, which offer federal tax incentives to encourage private investment in designated areas. Nine are on St. Croix, eight on St. Thomas, and one on St. John, and all 18 qualify as rural Opportunity Zones.

On St. Croix, the zones include parts of Christiansted, Frederiksted, Kingshill, and the South Shore, among them the former HOVENSA refinery and Renaissance properties. On St. Thomas, they include Tutu, Anna’s Retreat, Smith Bay, Crown Bay, Havensight, and Charlotte Amalie. Cruz Bay and nearby communities on St. John are included for the first time.

The designations take effect January 1, 2027, and last ten years. They are part of a new round the Treasury and the US Internal Revenue Service announced for more than 6,500 communities after the 2025 tax law made the incentive permanent. Investments in rural zones receive a 30% increase in their tax basis after five years, compared with 10% elsewhere. “Government cannot build this economy by itself,” Bryan said. “But getting the designation is only the beginning. What matters is turning those opportunities into real investments that benefit Virgin Islanders.”

Veterans Drive clears a federal hurdle

Bryan also announced an agreement with the US Coast Guard that removes a federal property obstacle to the second phase of the Veterans Drive Improvement Project on the Charlotte Amalie waterfront, a project the administration values at about $100 million. The first phase was completed in 2021. The second would widen the road around the Legislature of the US Virgin Islands to four lanes, add a tree-lined promenade, improve drainage, and strengthen the seawall.

The pre-solicitation period runs through November 19, and the solicitation period through January 13, 2027. Final property surveys, appraisals, and other approvals are still pending. Bryan, who leaves office when Governor-elect Stacey Plaskett (D) takes office on January 4, 2027, acknowledged the timeline. “We’re not going to finish every project before we leave office, but we can make sure the next administration has something solid to build on,” he said.

Faster payments for vendors, for a fee

Bryan also announced a voluntary partnership with Municipal Vendor Services Inc. (MVSI) that would let businesses that sell goods and services to the government get paid as soon as 72 hours after an invoice is approved. US Virgin Islands Government House said the program is meant to address longstanding concerns about late government payments, particularly among small businesses. “When you’re running a business, you have employees to pay and bills coming due. You can’t tell your employees to wait until the government pays you,” Bryan said. “We know our payment cycles have been a challenge.”

The program comes at a cost to vendors. MVSI Chief Executive Officer Theodore Ellenis told the St. Croix Source that the company would use lender financing to buy approved invoices, pay businesses 95% of their value, and collect the full amount from the government. A vendor with a $10,000 invoice would receive $9,500. Ellenis said the government would pay no added interest or fees. Bryan said the government pays 7.5% when it uses its bank line of credit to cover vendor payments.

The partnership has also drawn scrutiny. Municipal Vendor Services Inc., Ellenis, and Chief Financial Officer Robert Miragliotta are defendants in a federal securities lawsuit filed in New Jersey in March 2025 by Discover Growth Fund II, a fund based on St. Thomas, over its investment in an earlier company where the two executives held leadership roles. The territory’s agreement is with a separate entity, MVSI USVI SPE, LLC, which is not named in the suit, the Source reported. Ellenis disputed the allegations and said they do not affect the local program. Asked how much the government owes vendors, Bryan said he did not have the figure readily available.

item.title: Armed ICE agents enter Río Piedras parish grounds used by students as Puerto Rico weighs school protections

item.description:
Three armed ICE agents entered the courtyard of San Antonio de Padua Parish in Río Piedras, an area also used by its school’s students, 12 days before the Senate of Puerto Rico passed an amended bill on protections for students when ICE comes to public schools.

The post Armed ICE agents enter Río Piedras parish grounds used by students as Puerto Rico weighs school protections appeared first on Pasquines.
item.content:encoded:
Three armed US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents chasing two immigrants entered the courtyard of the San Antonio de Padua Parish in Río Piedras on October 24, 2026, as about 15 parishioners waited to go to confession, El Nuevo Día reported. The agents carried long guns and demanded to question workers who were repairing the church’s roof. The area they entered is also used by students of the parish’s school, Telemundo Puerto Rico reported.

A parishioner and the parish priest described the scene to El Nuevo Día. “They even searched the bathrooms,” one of them said. Archbishop Eusebio Ramos Morales of San Juan denounced the raid in an October 29 statement, saying that agents reaching the inner grounds of a parish showed they had exceeded their limits. “We say it very clearly: Enough!” he said.

Rebecca González Ramos, director of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), ICE’s investigative arm, said in November that her commitment not to carry out operations in schools or churches still stood. “Schools, hospitals, and churches are considered ‘sensitive locations.’ We respect that sensitive location,” she said. “If there has been any intervention at a church, a hospital, or a school, it is because there have been individuals who have run toward that periphery.” Governor Jenniffer González-Colón (NPP, R) said ICE operations in churches or schools were unnecessary. “They can wait for the person to leave a church,” she said on November 6.

The raid came 12 days before the Senate of Puerto Rico voted 20 to 4, on November 5, to pass Senate Bill 1062, which would write into law protections for students when ICE agents come to public schools. Before the vote, senators removed provisions that would have barred immigration interventions during class hours and required that a student be kept in a safe place while school officials checked whether an agent’s warrant was legal. The changes drew criticism from senators, civil liberties advocates, and members of the United States Congress, some of whom said the bill now offers less protection than the protocol the Puerto Rico Department of Education already follows.

The bill now goes to the Puerto Rico House of Representatives, where it had its first reading on November 11 and was referred to the House Education Committee. If the House passes it without changes, it will go to González-Colón, El Nuevo Día reported.

Puerto Ricans are US citizens by birth, but Puerto Rico falls under federal immigration law, and ICE has carried out operations on the islands since January 2025. By July 2025, ICE said it had detained 445 people in Puerto Rico, about 72% of them Dominican citizens. The Río Piedras raid came during operations led by ICE’s Enforcement and Removal Operations office in Miami across several San Juan neighborhoods from October 22 to 25, including Barrio Obrero, home to a large share of Puerto Rico’s Dominican community.

A protocol written after schools lost federal protection

On January 20, 2025, Acting United States Secretary of Homeland Security Benjamine Huffman rescinded guidelines that had limited ICE and US Customs and Border Protection enforcement in or near schools, churches, hospitals, and other “sensitive” areas. “Criminals will no longer be able to hide in America’s schools and churches to avoid arrest,” a department spokesperson said.

Days later, as the first large operations reached Puerto Rico, González Ramos, then the HSI special agent in charge in San Juan, said on the radio that agents did not plan to go into schools. “It is not our mission to enter any school, or any elder care site,” she said. Governor González-Colón said she had asked federal officials for a protocol for operations near churches, hospitals, and schools.

Attendance dropped anyway. By the end of January 2025, principals had reported absences of 20% to 60% at some schools with large numbers of foreign-born students, especially from the Dominican Republic, Secretary of Education Eliezer Ramos told WKAQ radio. The department declined to release specific figures, citing the safety of students and staff. “Schools are a sacred place of protection for our children,” Ramos said.

The Department of Education adopted its protocol in February 2025. It was reviewed by César Cedeño, then the Dominican Republic’s consul in Puerto Rico, and by González Ramos, and the Department of Education was the only Puerto Rico government agency that prepared one to protect this population, according to El Nuevo Día. Under the protocol, no minor can be detained without a court order, and the department’s Office of Legal Affairs must certify that an intervention is lawful. Schools cannot share information about a minor’s attendance or location without authorization from a parent, the regional superintendent, or the legal office. No minor can be questioned without a parent or legal guardian present or, failing that, a diplomatic representative of the student’s home country.

What the Senate changed

Senator Nitza Morán Trinidad (NPP) filed the bill on February 6, 2026, as the Educational Equity Law for Immigrant Students. Its statement of motives cites Plyler v. Doe, the 1982 US Supreme Court decision that states cannot deny free public education to undocumented students, and says the bill was inspired by guidance issued by New York State. “What we are seeking with this bill is to give those protections the force of law,” Morán said.

Most of the bill deals with enrollment and bullying. It would guarantee free public schooling regardless of immigration status, bar schools from asking for Social Security numbers or immigration status at enrollment, ban bullying over immigration status, and let families file complaints with the Department of Education or the Puerto Rico Civil Rights Commission. The Department of Education and the Department of the Family endorsed the committee report.

The fight was over Article 7, which governs what happens when agents arrive. The original version required a court order signed by a judge naming the student, and notice to the secretary of education before the order was carried out so the secretary could evaluate the intervention with the Puerto Rico Department of Justice. It gave students a right to have a parent and a lawyer present, required that they be kept “protected in a safe place at the school” while the order was validated, and barred any intervention during class hours.

The Senate Government Committee and the Education, Arts and Culture Committee rewrote that article in a joint report on October 29. The Government Committee held no public hearings, and its changes included language that would have let ICE enter schools with an administrative order issued by the agency itself rather than by a judge, Senator María de Lourdes Santiago Negrón (PIP) told NotiCel. Santiago recalled that ICE used an administrative subpoena in January 2025 to obtain the data of more than 6,000 immigrants who held Puerto Rico driver’s licenses.

Morán removed the administrative-order language on the Senate floor after objections from the minority parties. The approved text says an administrative order alone does not authorize school staff to give agents access to nonpublic areas, and it keeps a ban on staff voluntarily letting federal agents in without a court order.

Other changes stayed. The approved text says the Department of Education “may” consult the Department of Justice, and that notice and consultation are not prerequisites for federal action and cannot be used to delay it. Staff must only “seek” to have a parent present, to the extent the law allows. A student stays in a safe, supervised space “when circumstances allow,” and that space cannot be used to hide the student. Principals may ask that agents act outside classrooms, but the text says nothing in it bars legally authorized interventions during school hours. An earlier requirement to consult legal counsel before releasing student information was also removed.

The approved text also adds a clause on federal authority: “Nothing provided here shall have the effect of imposing additional conditions on the exercise of the powers conferred on federal authorities, requiring authorization from officials of the Government of Puerto Rico for the execution of legally authorized federal actions, or preventing, delaying, or obstructing their enforcement.”

Who voted against it

Eighteen senators of the New Progressive Party (NPP) and two of the Popular Democratic Party (PDP) voted for the bill, according to El Nuevo Día. The two senators of the Puerto Rican Independence Party (PIP), Santiago and Adrián González Costa, voted against it, as did independent senators Joanne Rodríguez Veve and Eliezer Molina Pérez. One senator abstained and three were absent, according to the Senate’s vote record.

“By definition, if you have to call someone or make a consultation, of course that is going to delay the intervention,” Santiago said. “That is the only way to guarantee protection for those girls and boys.”

González Costa, who said he had not opposed the bill before the committee rewrote it, objected to the federal authority clause. “That was not in the original version,” he said. “It is unfair to the secretary of education to say he favors it when he favored the original bill. They created a legal framework contrary to the protections the Department of Education has in place.”

Senator Luis Javier Hernández Ortiz (PDP), his party’s spokesperson in the Senate, was absent for the vote but said he agreed with the original version. “If you ask me, I would not have voted for the bill,” he said. The American Civil Liberties Union of Puerto Rico (ACLU) warned before the vote that the amendments compromised students’ constitutional rights. “No legislation aimed at protecting immigrant children should end up facilitating the very interventions it originally sought to protect them from,” the group said.

Opposition from New York and Washington

The vote drew attention from outside Puerto Rico. On November 6, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D), who was visiting the islands, said at a news conference that the amendments would let ICE into schools and threaten Puerto Rican children where they should be safest, El Nuevo Día reported. Juan Dalmau, secretary general of the PIP, said NPP and PDP senators had “made common cause to allow the most vulnerable and the most innocent, our children, to be subject to abuse and terror in the place that should be sacred, which is the schools.”

The same day, Representative Nydia Velázquez (D) of New York criticized NPP and PDP senators for backing the bill at a news conference at the Casa Dominicana in Villa Palmeras with Representative Adriano Espaillat (D) of New York and Resident Commissioner Pablo José Hernández Rivera (PDP, D). Velázquez condemned the raid at San Antonio de Padua and said that when the new Congress convenes in January, “ICE abuse is over,” referring to pending bills that would ban masks for immigration agents, require body cameras, and prohibit agents from entering schools or churches, El Nuevo Día reported. Democrats won majorities in both chambers in the November 3 midterm elections.

Hernández Rivera, who is also president of the PDP, said he wanted to see the final text before judging the senators of his party who voted for it, and that he would handle any differences internally. “Zero ICE in schools, in hospitals, in churches,” he said.

Former US Secretary of Education Miguel Cardona, who is Puerto Rican and served under President Joe Biden (D), weighed in on November 10. “For me, it is horrible to see ICE at school to take out children or parents or teachers. For me, it is a crime,” he said after giving the keynote at the annual gathering of Echar Pa’lante, a nonprofit that promotes partnerships among educators. “That keeps parents from trusting schools, and children don’t go to school when that happens.”

What comes next

Opponents of the amendments have pointed to the driver’s license case as a warning. The Puerto Rico Department of Transportation and Public Works gave federal agents the data of 6,321 immigrants after an administrative request from HSI, without a court order, and the ACLU has sued over it. González-Colón defended the handover. “There is a federal subpoena, and Puerto Rico government agencies have to comply with federal mandates,” she said.

It is not yet known whether the House will hold a public hearing on the bill, Claridad reported. In the meantime, the Department of Education’s February 2025 protocol remains in effect.
